extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in 19th-century American newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practices for producing and evaluating penny‑press newspapers in the 1830s–1860s (timeliness, audience selection, content mix, business/technical means). Focuses on what made early cheap dailies succeed or fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic view for the common people
rubrics_metrics.description: The great common people should have a realistic view of the contemporary scene, and this in spite of taboos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penny papers held that reporting should give working‑class readers an unvarnished sense of events even if that meant breaking earlier social taboos. This principle justified attention to topics previously avoided by 'respectable' papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose abuses in institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses in churches, courts, banks, stockmarkets, etc., should be exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the penny‑press creed was watchdog reporting that challenged established institutions; this could lead to libel suits and organized backlash but was central to the papers' reformist/assertive identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: First duty: give readers the news (not partisan/mercantile service)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper’s first duty is to give its readers the news, and not to support a party or a mercantile class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers claimed independence from party or commercial promoters, prioritizing what readers wanted over serving elite interests—though many later developed partisan slants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and human‑interest news is important
rubrics_metrics.description: Local and human‑interest news is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on home‑city items and stories about ordinary people (human‑interest) was a deliberate editorial choice to attract a broader, less 'respectable' readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience‑defined newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News is limited to those reports which the paper’s public wishes; the newspaper man’s definition of news is conditioned by what his public looks for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should select items based on the tastes and expectations of their target readers—shifting from elite 'important' topics (national politics, commerce) toward local, sensational, or human‑interest items that sell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on timeliness and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness as a feature of news—using steamships, railroads, and the magnetic telegraph to shorten transmission times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers competed on getting news faster via technological and logistical innovations (steamship intercepts, horse and locomotive expresses, telegraph lines). Investment in speed was a core competitive criterion for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enterprise in news‑gathering and special expresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of private expresses, carrier systems, boats meeting incoming vessels, carrier pigeons, and combinations among papers to secure fastest dispatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational enterprise—maintaining private boat services, horse/rail expresses, pigeon posts, or pooled services—was necessary to beat rivals on foreign and distant news; these measures often entailed significant expense or cooperative arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish broad correspondent/bureau networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a European correspondence, a Washington bureau, and correspondents in leading American cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building a network of correspondents and bureaus increased a paper’s capacity for original and timely reporting and was cited as a reason for circulation and influence growth (e.g., Herald’s European and Washington bureaus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational/crime/sex emphasis to attract mass readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A much greater emphasis on sensational news, especially that of crime and sex; police‑court columns and morbid details were widely used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational content was an explicit tactic to draw working‑class readers; editors used graphic police reports and scandal to sell copies. The text also notes this as an area open to abuse (overemphasis, possible falsification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humor and satire (society reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society items (parties of wealthy families, names obscured) spiced by satire—origins of the modern society page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing social gossip with satirical comment made society reporting entertaining and created new reader interest; editors used deliberate satire to engage and provoke readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or manage offense to sustain circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Promise more care to avoid offense after organized backlash; tone of the paper improved to recover lost circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive offensiveness (attacks on religion, personal scandals) could trigger organized boycotts and loss of readers; editors sometimes moderated tone or made public promises to regain credibility and circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial self‑promotion as a marketing tactic (and anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors (e.g., Bennett) advertised themselves—'selling' their own personality to the public; flamboyant self‑advertising anticipated showmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self‑promotion could increase a paper’s distinctiveness and sales but risked disgust among more 'fastidious' readers; excessive personalization of editorial content could be a liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management and pricing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise price strategically to fund improvements (example: Bennett raised price from one to two cents to finance expansion and better news service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound business calculations (weighing circulation losses vs. revenue gains) can finance presses, bureaus, and correspondents; pricing is a lever to balance reach and investment in quality/speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial caution and rigorous proofing to avoid impropriety/libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Look over every line of proof every day to make sure that nothing improper should be printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough editorial oversight (daily line‑by‑line proofing) was practiced to prevent libel and improper material; this is presented as an editorial standard that supported long‑term success (example: Swain of the Public Ledger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable/recognizable abuses: bad taste and disreputable advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad taste, coarseness which sometimes became indecency, overemphasis on crime and sex, and disreputable advertising were outstanding sins of these papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account treats these as recurring faults to be guarded against: while sensationalism sells, excessive indecency or sleazy ads damage reputation and invite backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: War correspondence practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For modern war coverage: maintain correspondents at the front, spend large sums for 'beats', use fast boats/composing rooms, and combine newspaper resources for expresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mexican War coverage exemplifies standards for conflict reporting—dedicated correspondents, logistical investment (boats, private expresses), and cooperative schemes to speed battlefield news to home papers.
